why: Cost and Usage Reports enabled in the Organizations management account automatically include usage for all member accounts, and CUR delivers natively to Amazon S3. Amazon Athena queries the CUR files in place with serverless, pay-per-query SQL, which is the most scalable and cost-effective choice for a once-a-month analysis.

others.A: CUR cannot be delivered to Kinesis, and running EMR for a monthly query adds cost and cluster management.
others.C: Enabling CUR per member account is unnecessary because the management account already sees consolidated billing data, and a Redshift cluster is costly for a monthly query.
others.D: CUR does not deliver to Kinesis, and per-member-account reports add needless effort.

tip: CUR + S3 + Athena is the standard pattern for ad hoc or periodic bill analysis; the management account's CUR covers all member accounts.

why: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and supports UDP listeners and target groups, and it can be attached to an Auto Scaling group so new instances are registered automatically as the group scales out and in.

others.B: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP/HTTPS (and gRPC) at layer 7 and cannot forward UDP traffic.
others.C: Route 53 weighted records do not register Auto Scaling instances dynamically or balance per-connection load.
others.D: A NAT instance is for outbound internet access from private subnets, not for load balancing inbound traffic, and it is a single point of failure.

tip: UDP, TCP, static IPs or extreme performance means NLB; HTTP path/host routing means ALB.

why: Storing logs in Amazon S3 is the cheapest durable storage for tens of GB per day, and Amazon Athena runs standard SQL directly on the S3 data with no infrastructure, charging only per query. Because analysis is only weekly and on demand, paying nothing between queries makes this the most cost-effective option.

others.B: Loading large volumes of logs into RDS requires a continuously running, provisioned database that is costly and not designed for log analytics at scale.
others.C: OpenSearch Service needs an always-on cluster sized for the data, which is expensive for weekly queries and is not standard SQL-first.
others.D: An EMR cluster storing data in HDFS must run continuously and requires cluster management, increasing cost.

tip: Infrequent, on-demand SQL over files in S3 = Athena.

why: A public ACM certificate is required for internet-facing TLS on an ALB, and one certificate can cover the apex example.com plus the wildcard *.example.com to secure every country subdomain. DNS validation by adding the CNAME records ACM provides proves domain ownership and lets ACM renew the certificate automatically.

others.B: Private certificates from ACM Private CA are not trusted by public browsers, so they are unsuitable for a public website.
others.C: Requesting both public and private certificates for only the apex domain does not cover the country subdomains, and the private one is unnecessary.
others.D: Email validation followed by switching to DNS validation is a confused, unnecessary step; you simply choose DNS validation when requesting.

tip: ACM public cert + DNS validation = automatic renewal; wildcard covers one subdomain level.

why: An AWS KMS external key store (XKS) lets KMS keys be backed by key material held in an external key manager outside AWS, reached via an XKS proxy, and it supports external key managers from multiple vendors. Applications keep using standard KMS APIs and integrated AWS services, giving the least operational overhead while keys never leave the on-premises manager.

others.A: A CloudHSM key store keeps keys inside AWS on CloudHSM hardware, violating the requirement that keys stay outside the AWS Cloud.
others.C: The default KMS key store holds keys in AWS-managed HSMs inside AWS, not in the company's external key manager.
others.D: A custom key store backed by CloudHSM still stores keys in AWS and adds HSM cluster management.

tip: Keys must stay outside AWS but use KMS = KMS External Key Store (XKS).

why: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a parallel, high-performance file system built for HPC with sub-millisecond latency and massive throughput across hundreds of instances. It can be linked to an S3 bucket via a data repository association so results are exported to S3 for later postprocessing.

others.A: EFS offers shared NFS access but is not designed for HPC-scale parallel throughput and its latency is generally higher than FSx for Lustre.
others.B: S3 is object storage; mounting it via tools does not provide a POSIX parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency.
others.D: AWS RAM shares resources across accounts and cannot make an S3 bucket mountable as a shared file system.

tip: HPC + parallel file system + S3 integration = FSx for Lustre.

why: AWS Global Accelerator gives users two static anycast IP addresses and routes traffic over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint, supporting UDP for VoIP. Its health checks fail over between Regions in seconds without depending on DNS changes, so client IP or DNS caching does not delay failover.

others.B: Route 53 geolocation routing depends on DNS, so failover is affected by DNS caching on clients, and it does not optimize the network path.
others.C: CloudFront is for HTTP/HTTPS content delivery and does not handle UDP-based VoIP traffic.
others.D: An ALB is a Regional resource with no cross-Region failover and does not support UDP.

tip: Non-HTTP (UDP/TCP) global traffic with fast Regional failover and static IPs = Global Accelerator.

why: FSx for Lustre provides sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s of throughput for thousands of concurrent compute instances. Persistent file systems replicate data within an Availability Zone and replace failed file servers automatically, meeting the high availability and sustained-throughput requirements.

others.A: Scratch file systems do not replicate data and are intended for temporary, short-term processing, so they are not highly available.
others.C: EFS Bursting mode cannot deliver sustained HPC throughput with sub-millisecond latency to thousands of instances.
others.D: EFS Provisioned Throughput still does not match the latency and parallel throughput of FSx for Lustre for HPC workloads.

tip: FSx for Lustre: scratch = cheap and temporary; persistent = durable and highly available.

why: gp3 volumes let you provision IOPS (up to 16,000 on RDS gp3 depending on storage size thresholds) and throughput independently of storage capacity at a lower price than io1. Since the peak does not exceed 15,000 IOPS, gp3 is the most cost-effective choice.

others.A: gp2 IOPS scale with volume size (3 IOPS per GB) and cannot be provisioned independently of capacity.
others.B: io1 can provide 15,000 IOPS independently but costs significantly more per GB and per IOPS than gp3.
others.D: Magnetic storage is legacy, offers very low IOPS, and cannot meet 15,000 IOPS.

tip: Need IOPS independent of size cheaply = gp3; io1/io2 only when you need beyond gp3 limits or higher durability.

why: Amazon RDS for SQL Server is a managed service that supports the Enterprise edition, so the database can be migrated without rewriting the application. RDS for SQL Server read replicas (Enterprise edition) offload reporting queries from the production instance, minimizing operational overhead.

others.B: Running SQL Server on EC2 with Always On requires managing the OS, patching, backups and clustering yourself, which is more overhead.
others.C: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database; migrating a relational SQL Server workload requires a full redesign, and on-demand replicas are not a reporting feature.
others.D: Migrating to Aurora MySQL requires schema and code conversion from T-SQL, adding significant effort.

tip: Managed + minimal change for SQL Server = RDS for SQL Server; read replicas for reporting.

why: S3 Standard-IA stores data across multiple Availability Zones, so images will not be lost, and it is cheaper for infrequently accessed objects after 180 days. Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access for archived data after 360 days, and Glacier Deep Archive's standard retrieval within 12 hours suits auditor access after 5 years at the lowest cost.

others.A: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so an AZ loss could lose images, violating the durability requirement.
others.B: One Zone-IA risks data loss, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval does not provide instant access after 360 days.
others.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours to restore, failing the instant-availability requirement after 360 days.

tip: Archive but instant access = Glacier Instant Retrieval; retrieval within 12 hours = Deep Archive.

why: A transient EMR cluster runs only for the 6-hour daily job and then terminates, avoiding paying for idle capacity. Keeping the primary and core nodes on On-Demand Instances protects HDFS data and cluster state from Spot interruptions, while task nodes (compute only, no HDFS) can safely use cheaper Spot Instances.

others.A: A long-running cluster pays for capacity during the 18 idle hours each day, which is less cost-effective.
others.C: Core nodes store HDFS data; running them on Spot risks data loss if instances are reclaimed.
others.D: Long-running wastes money and Spot core nodes risk losing data.

tip: EMR: primary and core on On-Demand for reliability, task nodes on Spot; transient clusters for periodic jobs.

why: CloudTrail records every resource-creation API call along with the identity of the caller, and an EventBridge rule can match those events and invoke a Lambda function in near real time. The function looks up the caller's cost center in the RDS database and applies the correct tag to the new resource.

others.A: SCPs can deny actions lacking tags but cannot look up a user's cost center or add tags, and existing resources cannot be required to be tagged before they are created.
others.C: A scheduled rule invoking a CloudFormation stack is not event-driven and does not tie resources to the user who created them.
others.D: Tagging with a default value does not meet the requirement to use each creator's cost center ID.

tip: React to API activity = CloudTrail event -> EventBridge rule -> Lambda.

why: CloudFront with an S3 origin serves the static content in a highly available, managed way. The PHP application runs on ECS with Fargate behind an ALB across multiple AZs, and sessions move to a Multi-AZ ElastiCache for Redis cluster so any task can serve any user, giving a highly available design built on managed services.

others.A: A single Elastic Beanstalk EC2 instance in a public subnet is not highly available and does not externalize the Redis session store.
others.B: Lambda does not natively host a traditional Apache/PHP application without significant refactoring, and serving static content through Lambda is inefficient.
others.C: The backend stays on a single EC2 instance, which remains a single point of failure.

tip: HA redesign: static to S3/CloudFront, stateless compute behind ALB, sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB.

why: An Application Load Balancer supports sticky sessions through load-balancer-generated or application cookies on its target groups and can be public. AWS WAF web ACLs can be associated directly with an ALB, adding layer 7 protection to the endpoint.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer, so it cannot meet the WAF requirement.
others.B: A Gateway Load Balancer is for inline third-party virtual appliances, not for exposing a public web application with sticky sessions.
others.D: A second target group and Elastic IPs add nothing toward WAF protection or session affinity.

tip: AWS WAF attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito and App Runner, not NLB.

why: Images accessed only once or twice a year are a good fit for S3 Standard-IA, which has a lower storage price than S3 Standard while keeping millisecond access and multi-AZ high availability. S3 can serve the objects directly, so no servers are needed and it is the most cost-effective option.

others.A: EBS is tied to a single instance and AZ and needs a running EC2 web server, which is costly and not highly available.
others.B: EFS plus EC2 web servers costs more for storage and compute than S3 for rarely accessed images.
others.C: S3 Standard works but costs more for storage than Standard-IA for objects that are rarely accessed.

tip: Rarely accessed but needs immediate access and multi-AZ durability = S3 Standard-IA.

why: A customer managed prefix list holds the office CIDRs in one place, and AWS RAM can share it with the whole organization. Security groups in every account reference the prefix list, so adding or removing a CIDR is a single edit that propagates everywhere at no extra cost.

others.A: Security groups are VPC- and account-scoped and cannot be used directly by other accounts' resources, so this does not centralize rules.
others.C: AWS managed prefix lists are for AWS service ranges and cannot be edited by customers, and Security Hub does not enforce security group content.
others.D: Firewall Manager can centralize security groups but carries per-policy charges and requires additional setup, so it is less cost-effective than a shared prefix list.

tip: Shared list of CIDRs across accounts = customer managed prefix list shared via AWS RAM.

why: A cluster placement group packs instances close together in one AZ for the lowest network latency and highest throughput between nodes, which suits latency-sensitive HPC. Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the FSx option that provides simultaneous NFS and SMB multi-protocol access to the same data.

others.B: Partition placement groups spread instances across racks for fault isolation (e.g. HDFS, Cassandra), not for lowest latency.
others.C: FSx for Lustre is POSIX/Lustre-client based and does not provide SMB access.
others.D: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS (and SMB is not native for multi-protocol access), so it does not meet the NFS plus SMB requirement.

tip: NFS + SMB on the same file system = FSx for NetApp ONTAP; lowest inter-node latency = cluster placement group.

why: With the VPN already 90% utilized, transferring 50 TB online in 2 weeks is impractical. A Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device holds around 80 TB usable, encrypts data with KMS-managed keys, and is shipped to AWS, meeting the secure 2-week transfer requirement.

others.A: DataSync would still use the nearly saturated VPN link, which cannot move 50 TB in 2 weeks.
others.B: Provisioning a new Direct Connect connection often takes weeks or months, risking the 2-week deadline, and is costly for a one-time move.
others.D: Storage Gateway also relies on the existing saturated network link and is designed for hybrid access rather than bulk migration.

tip: Tens of TB, limited bandwidth, short deadline = Snowball Edge.

why: Peak hours occur at the same time every day, so a scheduled scaling action can add instances before the peak begins. This avoids the lag of reactive dynamic scaling, so capacity is already in service when users arrive.

others.A: An ALB distributes load but does not add the capacity that is missing at the start of the peak.
others.B: Dynamic scaling on memory reacts only after load rises (and requires a custom metric), so slowness at the start of peak persists.
others.C: Dynamic scaling on CPU also reacts after demand increases, causing the same warm-up delay.

tip: Predictable, recurring load = scheduled scaling (or predictive scaling).

why: Amazon RDS Proxy is a fully managed connection pooler that shares and reuses database connections, absorbing connection spikes as applications scale out. Applications only need to point to the proxy endpoint, which gives the least operational overhead.

others.A: Moving to DynamoDB requires redesigning the data model and application, and DynamoDB does not use connection pooling target groups.
others.C: A custom proxy on EC2 must be built, scaled, patched and made highly available by the company.
others.D: Lambda is not a connection pooler and would add complexity and latency for every database request.

tip: Too many DB connections from scaling apps or Lambda = RDS Proxy.

why: Growing snapshot costs come from accumulating snapshots. Deleting nonessential snapshots cuts current costs, and Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshot creation and retention so old snapshots are deleted per policy, with minimal ongoing effort.

others.A: EBS Elastic Volumes cannot decrease volume size, and CloudWatch Logs does not natively report EBS disk usage.
others.B: A custom script adds operational overhead, and Elastic Volumes cannot shrink volumes.
others.C: A one-time deletion helps but does not prevent snapshots from accumulating again, so costs will keep rising.

tip: Automate EBS snapshot retention = Data Lifecycle Manager (or AWS Backup).

why: A customer managed KMS key lets the company control exactly which principals can use the key through its key policy. Encrypting both the S3 bucket and the RDS database with this key and granting encrypt/decrypt only to the ECS task role restricts who can use the key material.

others.B: AWS managed keys have key policies that cannot be edited, so access cannot be limited to the ECS role, and naming a role as a 'user' in a bucket policy is not meaningful.
others.C: An RDS interface VPC endpoint is for the RDS management API, not database connections, so it does not restrict data access.
others.D: The RDS VPC endpoint again covers only the management API, so this does not control database data access as intended.

tip: Only a customer managed key lets you edit the key policy. Note: RDS decrypts transparently for any authenticated DB user, so network and DB auth controls still matter in practice.

why: Burstable (T-family) instances in unlimited mode can sustain CPU well above baseline whenever needed, absorbing the instant 10x CPU spike while new instances launch. Scaling the Elastic Beanstalk environment on requests adds capacity automatically when demand increases.

others.B: Compute optimized instances cost more for a workload that is normally low, and they cannot instantly absorb a 10x spike before scaling completes.
others.C: Scheduled scaling does not fit spikes that are not tied to known times, and compute optimized instances are over-provisioned for normal load.
others.D: Predictive scaling needs regular, cyclical patterns with enough history; two spikes a month are a poor fit.

tip: T instances in unlimited mode handle unpredictable CPU bursts without credit exhaustion.

why: AWS CloudFormation provisions the infrastructure as code, automating secure, repeatable deployments. AWS Config records configuration changes to resources over time, giving the security team a timeline of incremental changes to track and audit.

others.A: AWS Organizations manages accounts and policies; it does not provision infrastructure.
others.C: Organizations does not provision infrastructure, and Service Catalog does not track configuration changes.
others.D: Service Catalog publishes approved products but does not audit incremental resource configuration changes.

tip: Provision = CloudFormation; record and audit config changes = AWS Config; who made the API call = CloudTrail.

why: Migrating MySQL to RDS Multi-AZ gives a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover, without code changes. Placing the stateless Python application in an Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB removes the single-instance point of failure.

others.A: An internet gateway is a highly available, VPC-level resource; you cannot and need not create one per AZ.
others.C: Moving to DynamoDB requires changing the application code, which is not allowed.
others.D: DataSync transfers files; it is not a database replication or HA mechanism.

tip: Classic HA combo: ALB + multi-AZ Auto Scaling group + RDS Multi-AZ.

why: S3 interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) have private IP addresses in the VPC, so they can be reached from on premises over Direct Connect as well as from within the Region. Traffic stays on private connectivity and does not traverse the internet.

others.A: S3 gateway endpoints work only for traffic originating in the VPC and cannot be used from on-premises networks.
others.B: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and networks but does not itself provide private access to S3.
others.D: A KMS key provides encryption, not a private network path, so traffic could still traverse the internet.

tip: On-prem private access to S3 = interface endpoint; in-VPC only and free = gateway endpoint.

why: An Organizations tag policy can define the application name tag key and its allowed values, and with enforcement enabled for specified resource types, noncompliant tagging operations are prevented. It applies centrally across all accounts in the organization.

others.A: IAM groups are not used with IAM Identity Center users in member accounts, and per-account IAM policies are harder to manage centrally across the organization.
others.B: A Deny for resources that have the tag would block the correctly tagged resources, the opposite of the goal.
others.C: Resource Groups organizes and views resources; it does not validate or enforce tag values.

tip: Standardize allowed tag values across an organization = tag policies (often paired with an SCP requiring the tag).

why: AWS Secrets Manager integrates natively with RDS (including RDS-managed master user passwords) and provides built-in automatic rotation on a schedule such as every 30 days. No custom code is required, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.A: A custom Lambda function on an EventBridge schedule must be written and maintained, adding overhead.
others.B: Running modify-db-instance manually is not automated and the new password still has to be stored securely.
others.D: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation for RDS credentials.

tip: Automatic credential rotation = Secrets Manager; Parameter Store has no native rotation.

why: The tests have known, steady read and write rates, so provisioned mode can be set to exactly that capacity during the 4-hour window and lowered afterward. Provisioned capacity costs less per request than on-demand when utilization is predictable.

others.A: On-demand mode does not use read and write capacity unit settings, and it is priced higher per request for a known, steady load.
others.C: Reserved capacity requires a 1-year commitment for continuous capacity, wasteful for 4 hours a week.
others.D: A 3-year reservation is even more wasteful for a weekly 4-hour test.

tip: Known, predictable throughput = provisioned mode; unknown or spiky = on-demand.

why: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to monitor spending patterns continuously and sends alerts through email or SNS to stakeholders when unusual spend is detected. This directly meets the requirement to monitor costs and notify on anomalies.

others.A: A zero spend budget alerts on any spend at all, which is not useful for an account that already runs workloads.
others.C: Pricing Calculator produces estimates; it does not monitor actual spend or notify anyone.
others.D: CloudWatch billing alarms only alert on fixed thresholds and do not identify unusual spending patterns.

tip: Unusual or unexpected spend = Cost Anomaly Detection; fixed thresholds = AWS Budgets.

why: An AWS Glue crawler infers the schema of the clickstream data and registers tables in the Glue Data Catalog. Amazon Athena can then query the data in S3 immediately with serverless SQL, giving a quick analysis with the least operational overhead.

others.A: Writing and running Glue Spark jobs to query data requires more development effort than ad hoc Athena SQL.
others.C: Running EMR with a Hive metastore and Spark jobs requires cluster management.
others.D: Kinesis Data Analytics is for streaming data, not for querying data already at rest in S3.

tip: Quick SQL on S3 data = Glue crawler + Athena.

why: Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an SMB share backed by S3 and caches recently used files locally for fast access during the first 7 days. An S3 Lifecycle rule then moves objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, whose standard retrieval completes within 12 hours (bulk within 48), meeting the 24-hour retrieval limit at the lowest cost.

others.A: DataSync only copies data; it does not provide ongoing SMB access or a tiering policy for older files.
others.C: FSx File Gateway caches FSx for Windows File Server shares, which do not support S3 Lifecycle transitions.
others.D: Giving each user direct S3 access breaks the SMB file-share workflow and adds per-user administration.

tip: SMB/NFS on premises backed by S3 with lifecycle tiering = S3 File Gateway.

why: A read replica offloads read queries from the primary RDS for PostgreSQL instance, and the application can send read traffic to it. ElastiCache caches frequently requested query results in memory, further reducing database read load and latency during traffic spikes.

others.A: RDS storage auto scaling only grows storage; it does not add compute for read load.
others.C: The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve read traffic.
others.E: Placing instances in the same AZ as the database reduces resilience and does not address read load.

tip: Read-heavy RDS = read replicas and/or ElastiCache; Multi-AZ instance standby is for HA only.

why: EBS Snapshot Lock lets you lock snapshots for a retention period (governance or compliance mode) so they cannot be deleted, regardless of the user's IAM permissions. It is applied directly to the snapshots, so the storage administrator's rights are unchanged and effort is minimal.

others.A: Creating a role and EC2 instance for deletions adds effort and does not prevent the administrator from deleting snapshots.
others.B: Attaching a deny policy changes the storage administrator's administrative rights, which is not allowed.
others.C: Recycle Bin allows recovery after deletion rather than preventing deletion, and requires tagging every snapshot.

tip: Prevent deletion = Snapshot Lock; recover after accidental deletion = Recycle Bin.

why: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic information for network interfaces and can publish to a CloudWatch Logs log group. A subscription filter can stream that log group to Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers to OpenSearch Service natively in near real time without custom consumers.

others.A: Kinesis Data Streams cannot write directly to OpenSearch; it would require custom consumer code.
others.C: CloudTrail records API calls, not network traffic, and Flow Logs cannot be sent to a trail.
others.D: Flow Logs cannot be delivered to CloudTrail, so this pipeline does not exist.

tip: Firehose has native delivery to OpenSearch, S3, Redshift and Splunk; Data Streams needs consumers.

why: Using two managed node groups, one On-Demand and one Spot, keeps the nodes fully managed by EKS while cutting cost with Spot capacity. The On-Demand group keeps baseline cluster components running when Spot Instances are interrupted, allowing resiliency testing of the application.

others.A: An all-Spot node group is cheapest but risks losing all nodes at once during interruptions, leaving the cluster unable to run baseline workloads.
others.C: A self-managed Auto Scaling group with user data is not managed by EKS and uses deprecated launch configurations.
others.D: An all On-Demand node group is the most expensive option for an infrequently used dev cluster.

tip: Cost-optimized EKS: mix On-Demand for baseline with Spot node groups for the rest.

why: A customer managed KMS key gives the company full control over key creation, key policies, rotation (automatic or on demand) and enabling or disabling the key. SSE-KMS applies that key to S3 objects transparently, so encryption requires minimal effort.

others.A: With SSE-S3, AWS manages the keys and users cannot create, rotate or disable them.
others.C: Customers cannot create AWS managed keys or control their rotation or disabling; AWS creates and manages them.
others.D: Downloading, encrypting and re-uploading objects through EC2 is high effort and error prone.

tip: Need control over rotate/disable/policy = customer managed KMS key.

why: S3 Object Lock (which requires versioning and is enabled on the bucket) with a default retention period of 30 days prevents the backups from being deleted or overwritten during that period. An S3 Lifecycle expiration rule then deletes the objects automatically after 30 days.

others.B: Versioning alone does not prevent deletion and is enabled automatically when Object Lock is enabled.
others.D: Lifecycle policies cannot protect objects from deletion; they only transition or expire them.
others.F: Tags do not enforce any retention; S3 does not act on a tag value as a lock.

tip: Retain (WORM) = Object Lock retention; delete afterwards = Lifecycle expiration.

why: AWS DataSync supports S3 as a source and both S3 and EFS as destinations, and tasks can run on a schedule for continuous copying. Setting the transfer mode to transfer only data that has changed means destination files are overwritten only when the source changes, all with a managed service.

others.B: A custom Lambda function with EFS mount and event notifications must be built and maintained, adding operational overhead.
others.C: Transferring all data every time wastes time and bandwidth and rewrites unchanged files.
others.D: An EC2 instance with a sync script requires managing servers and custom code.

tip: Managed recurring copy between S3, EFS, FSx = DataSync with changed-data-only mode.

why: A customer managed KMS key lets the company enable automatic rotation and choose the rotation period, or rotate on demand, giving it control of rotation. EBS encryption with that key is native and transparent, so operational overhead is low.

others.B: AWS managed keys rotate automatically every year on AWS's schedule and the customer cannot configure their rotation.
others.C: Imported key material does not support automatic rotation, so rotation must be done manually, adding overhead.
others.D: AWS owned keys are fully controlled by AWS and are not visible to or controllable by the customer.

tip: Control rotation with least effort = customer managed key with automatic rotation.

why: An IAM policy using the ec2:Encrypted condition can block creation of unencrypted EBS volumes. AWS Config's managed rule encrypted-volumes detects noncompliant volumes automatically, and its remediation actions run Systems Manager Automation documents to fix findings, with little custom work.

others.B: KMS controls key access but does not detect unencrypted volumes, and Lambda plus EventBridge requires custom detection and remediation code.
others.C: Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it does not assess EBS volume encryption.
others.D: Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, not EBS encryption compliance.

tip: Detect and auto-remediate noncompliant config = AWS Config rules + SSM Automation remediation.

why: Moving the web tier to EC2 in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB is a lift-and-shift that adds self-healing and multi-AZ resiliency. Migrating MySQL to RDS Multi-AZ keeps the same engine with minimal changes and adds automatic failover to a standby.

others.B: A single-node MySQL database cannot simply be scaled behind an NLB; multiple independent instances would not share consistent data.
others.D: Rewriting the web tier as Lambda functions requires significant application changes.
others.E: DynamoDB is NoSQL and would require rewriting the data layer.

tip: Minimal change + resiliency = EC2 ASG/ALB and RDS Multi-AZ.

why: AWS Local Zones are extensions of a parent Region placed in metro areas, letting you extend the VPC from eu-central-1 into a Local Zone in a different location. Workloads run outside the eu-central-1 Region itself, satisfying the regulatory constraint, while still achieving single-digit millisecond latency for nearby users.

others.A: CloudFront edge locations cache content; you cannot extend a VPC or run applications in them.
others.C: Regional edge caches are part of CloudFront's caching tier and cannot host VPC workloads.
others.D: Wavelength Zones are embedded in telecom 5G networks for mobile-device latency, not general on-premises web application migration.

tip: Low latency to a metro area via VPC extension = Local Zones; 5G mobile edge = Wavelength.

why: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, so bursts of Lambda invocations do not open too many connections and database performance stays predictable. Because the RDS instance is private, the Lambda functions must be attached to the VPC to reach the proxy endpoint.

others.A: RDS custom endpoints are an Aurora feature for grouping instances and do not pool connections.
others.C: Custom endpoints do not pool connections, and Lambda outside the VPC cannot reach a private database.
others.D: RDS Proxy is only reachable from within the VPC, so Lambda outside the VPC cannot use it.

tip: Lambda + relational DB connection storms = RDS Proxy, Lambda in the VPC.

why: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a regional hub: VPCs attach with VPC attachments and on-premises sites with Site-to-Site VPN attachments. New accounts and VPCs are added with a single attachment (and can be shared via AWS RAM), avoiding a mesh of peering connections and scaling with minimal administration.

others.A: VPC peering is non-transitive and grows as a full mesh, and per-VPC VPNs multiply connections to manage.
others.B: A self-managed VPN EC2 instance is a single point of failure and requires ongoing management.
others.D: Peering is non-transitive, so on-premises traffic cannot route through the central VPC to other peered VPCs.

tip: Many VPCs + on-prem sites, scaling = Transit Gateway hub.

why: Amazon Forecast is a fully managed time-series forecasting service that requires no ML expertise: you import historical data from S3 and train a predictor. A Lambda function with a function URL can then query the Forecast predictor to return predictions for given inputs.

others.A: Deploying SageMaker models and endpoints requires ML knowledge to build, tune and host models.
others.B: Training a model in SageMaker requires choosing algorithms and ML expertise the company lacks.
others.C: Using SageMaker endpoints depends on building and deploying a custom model, which requires ML experience.

tip: Time-series forecasting without ML expertise = Amazon Forecast. Note: AWS closed Forecast to new customers in 2024; SageMaker Canvas is now the suggested no-code alternative.

why: With IAM Identity Center, you create groups for developers and administrators, define permission sets containing the needed policies, and assign each group plus permission set to the appropriate accounts. New hires simply join a group to inherit all access across accounts, minimizing ongoing effort.

others.A: Identity Center users are not created per account, and custom IAM policies per group do not use permission sets for multi-account access.
others.B: Attaching managed policies to each user individually does not scale and ignores permission sets.
others.D: Per-user permission sets and extra per-account IAM grants create high ongoing administrative overhead.

tip: Multi-account access with Identity Center: groups + permission sets assigned to accounts.

why: AWS Config's managed rule encrypted-volumes continuously evaluates EBS volumes and flags any that are not encrypted. It needs no custom code or compute, so it minimizes both cost and configuration effort while standardizing the encryption check.

others.A: A scheduled Lambda function with custom API calls must be written, tested and maintained.
others.B: Running custom checks on Fargate tasks adds code, scheduling and compute costs.
others.C: Tags and Cost Explorer do not indicate encryption status, and manual encryption is error prone.

tip: Continuous compliance checks on resource configuration = AWS Config managed rules.

why: S3 multipart upload splits large files into parts uploaded in parallel, raising upload throughput from on premises. Byte-range fetches download multiple ranges of the same object in parallel, scaling download throughput to the EC2 instances.

others.A: Access points simplify access control; they do not increase transfer throughput.
others.B: Spreading files across buckets adds complexity and does not speed up individual large transfers.
others.E: Random prefixes are no longer needed since S3 scales to 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET requests per second per prefix, and they do not speed up single large files.

tip: Big uploads = multipart; big downloads = parallel byte-range GETs.

why: Amazon EFS is a shared, multi-AZ file system that provides strong read-after-write consistency to all mounted EC2 instances. S3 also provides strong read-after-write consistency, and setting Cache-Control: no-cache makes CloudFront revalidate with the origin so the newest content is returned immediately.

others.A: Volume Gateway iSCSI volumes are block storage for on-premises use and cannot be shared safely across multiple EC2 instances.
others.C: EBS volumes are AZ-scoped, and Multi-Attach is limited to io1/io2 in one AZ and requires a cluster-aware file system.
others.D: DataSync runs scheduled transfers and does not provide immediate, strongly consistent shared storage.

tip: Shared file storage across AZs = EFS; S3 is strongly consistent for reads after writes.

why: A Route 53 latency-based routing policy sends each user to the Region with the lowest measured network latency for that user, providing the best performance. An A record (alias) can point to each Region's ALB.

others.B: Geolocation routes by the user's location for compliance or localization, which does not always give the lowest latency.
others.C: Failover routing is active-passive for disaster recovery, not performance across three active Regions.
others.D: Geoproximity routes by geographic distance with bias, which is not the same as measured latency, and needs Traffic Flow.

tip: 'Best performance' across Regions in Route 53 = latency routing.

why: Spreading the Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones makes the web tier highly available. Migrating the embedded NoSQL database to DynamoDB with AWS DMS gives a fully managed, multi-AZ database that supports eventually consistent reads, removing database management overhead.

others.A: An NLB does not improve availability over an ALB here, and the instances remain in one AZ with a self-managed database.
others.B: Swapping to an NLB does not fix the single-AZ compute tier.
others.C: Keeping the embedded database replication on EC2 means managing database replication and recovery yourself.

tip: HA = multiple AZs; least overhead for NoSQL = DynamoDB.

why: ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond in-memory access for caching the slowly changing catalog from DynamoDB. It also stores shopping cart and session data outside the web servers, with Multi-AZ replication for high availability, so the cart persists when a user disconnects and reconnects to any server.

others.A: Sticky sessions tie users to one instance, so cart data is lost if that instance fails, and Aurora is not a low-latency cache.
others.C: OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, not a low-latency session or cache store.
others.D: A single EC2 instance with EBS is a single point of failure and does not scale with traffic.

tip: Externalize session state to ElastiCache (Redis) or DynamoDB for HA and scaling.

why: CloudWatch Container Insights collects, aggregates and summarizes metrics and logs from EKS clusters, nodes, pods and services. AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing of requests across the microservices, revealing latency and errors between services.

others.A: ElastiCache reduces load but provides no observability into performance issues.
others.C: CloudTrail logs AWS API calls, not application-level requests between microservices.
others.D: Trusted Advisor gives account-level best-practice checks, not application performance insight.

tip: Metrics for containers = Container Insights; request tracing across services = X-Ray.

why: A separate KMS key per customer with SSE-KMS encrypts each customer's data at rest. Each key policy can deny kms:Decrypt to all principals except the customer's IAM role (cross-account), so only that customer can decrypt their data and company employees cannot.

others.A: ACM certificates are for TLS, not data encryption, and ACM has no certificate policies controlling decryption.
others.B: S3 bucket policies cannot control KMS decryption permissions; decryption rights are governed by the KMS key policy.
others.D: Public ACM certificates cannot be used to encrypt data and have no such access policy.

tip: Who can decrypt is controlled by the KMS key policy; per-tenant keys isolate tenants.

why: An internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets receives internet traffic on ports 80 and 443 and forwards it to the EC2 instance in the private subnet registered in its target group. Pointing DNS at the ALB keeps the instance private, meeting the mandate.

others.A: An Auto Scaling group identifier is not a DNS target, and instances in a private subnet remain unreachable from the internet.
others.C: A NAT gateway only allows outbound traffic from private subnets and must sit in a public subnet; it does not accept inbound connections.
others.D: Instances in a private subnet have no route from the internet gateway, so security group rules and a public IP will not help.

tip: Private instances serving the internet = public ALB/NLB in front; NAT is outbound only.

why: Amazon EFS is a regional, multi-AZ file system that can be mounted by many pods concurrently, and EKS on Fargate supports EFS through the EFS CSI driver. Registering it in a StorageClass and sharing one file system gives highly available, shared persistent storage with minimal management.

others.A: Fargate pods cannot mount EBS volumes, and EBS Multi-Attach is limited to a single AZ.
others.C: An EBS volume lives in one AZ and cannot be shared across pods on Fargate, so it is neither shared nor fault tolerant.
others.D: Multiple EFS file systems synchronized by Lambda add unnecessary complexity; a single EFS file system is already multi-AZ.

tip: Fargate persistent shared storage = EFS.

why: ECS with the Fargate launch type removes all server management, and Amazon EFS volumes can be mounted into Fargate tasks as persistent, shared storage that AWS fully manages. This meets the no-servers, no-storage-infrastructure requirement.

others.A: Self-managed EKS nodes and an EC2-attached EBS volume require managing servers and storage.
others.C: S3 cannot be mapped natively as a persistent volume in ECS task definitions; it is object storage, not a file system mount.
others.D: The EC2 launch type requires the company to manage the container instances.

tip: Serverless containers needing persistent volumes = Fargate + EFS.

why: Network Load Balancers handle both TCP and UDP traffic in each Region. AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes users over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy Regional NLB endpoint, giving low latency and fast cross-Region failover.

others.B: Application Load Balancers do not support UDP.
others.D: Geolocation routing relies on DNS and does not optimize latency or provide fast failover.
others.E: CloudFront serves HTTP/HTTPS traffic and does not proxy arbitrary TCP and UDP game traffic.

tip: Global TCP+UDP with HA and low latency = Global Accelerator + NLBs.

why: AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection for ALBs, detailed attack diagnostics and reporting that serves as an audit trail, and access to the Shield Response Team (formerly DRT) to apply mitigations. It requires minimal configuration changes to the existing architecture.

others.A: WAF rules blocking 'unknown sources' are impractical for random IPs and do not give DDoS attack diagnostics.
others.B: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability scanner, and the DDoS Response Team is only available with Shield Advanced.
others.D: Adding CloudFront changes the architecture and DNS, and WAF alone lacks DDoS attack reporting and expert response.

tip: DDoS protection + attack visibility + expert response team = Shield Advanced.

why: Snowball Edge devices import data into Amazon S3. Linking an FSx for Lustre file system to the S3 bucket presents the data to the HPC cluster as a high-throughput parallel file system with consistent sub-millisecond latency, lazily loading or preloading objects from S3.

others.A: Storage Gateway file gateway is for on-premises access to S3 and does not deliver HPC-grade throughput and latency in AWS.
others.C: EFS does not match FSx for Lustre performance for HPC, and copying 200 TB adds time and cost.
others.D: Snowball Edge import jobs land data in S3, not directly into an FSx for Lustre file system.

tip: Snowball imports to S3; then FSx for Lustre linked to S3 for HPC.

why: AWS DataSync uses an on-premises agent to read from NFS shares and transfer data to S3 on a schedule, with incremental transfers, encryption and integrity checks. Paying per GB transferred makes it cost-effective for small periodic backups.

others.A: AWS Glue is an ETL service and cannot read from on-premises NFS servers for backup.
others.C: Transfer Family incurs hourly endpoint charges and requires an SFTP client workflow, making it costlier and less suitable.
others.D: Direct Connect is expensive and slow to provision for small, periodic backups.

tip: Scheduled NFS/SMB to S3 transfers = DataSync.

why: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4, supports UDP, and can handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency. Registering the game server EC2 instances as targets provides this cost-effectively.

others.A: Application Load Balancers do not support UDP.
others.B: Gateway Load Balancers are for inline virtual appliances such as firewalls, not distributing client traffic to game servers.
others.D: Duplicating servers across Regions increases cost and does not by itself load balance UDP traffic.

tip: UDP + millions of requests per second + low latency = NLB.

why: Moving from MySQL to PostgreSQL is a heterogeneous migration, so DMS Schema Conversion is used to convert the schema and database objects to Aurora PostgreSQL. A DMS task with full load plus change data capture (CDC) then copies the data and continuously replicates ongoing changes until cutover.

others.B: DMS Schema Conversion converts schemas; it cannot create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica of an RDS for MySQL instance.
others.C: An Aurora MySQL read replica keeps the MySQL engine, not the required PostgreSQL target.
others.E: Cross-engine Aurora PostgreSQL read replicas of RDS for MySQL do not exist, so there is nothing to promote.

tip: Heterogeneous migration = schema conversion (DMS SC/SCT) + DMS full load and CDC.

why: A read replica serves read-only queries from an asynchronously replicated copy, so pointing the reporting script at it removes the load from the primary. It is a simple configuration change with low cost and no code complexity.

others.A: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby cannot be read, so the script cannot pick a less busy instance; this also requires custom logic.
others.C: Manual daily exports are labor intensive and error prone.
others.D: Caching rarely helps a script that looks for new entries, and it adds a service plus application changes.

tip: Offload reporting reads = read replica.

why: ALB access logs record each request's client IP, path, latency, status codes and user agent, delivered to S3. Defining an Athena table over the logs lets you run SQL queries to analyze abnormal patterns without managing any infrastructure.

others.A: CloudTrail captures AWS API calls, not HTTP requests reaching the ALB.
others.C: Manually searching log files in a text editor is not operationally efficient.
others.D: EMR cannot query an ALB directly, and running a cluster adds overhead.

tip: Analyze ALB/CloudFront/VPC logs in S3 = Athena.

why: A public NAT gateway must be placed in a public subnet (one with a route to the internet gateway) and has an Elastic IP. Private subnet route tables send 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway, allowing outbound internet access.

others.A: A public NAT gateway in a private subnet has no route to the internet gateway, so traffic cannot reach the internet.
others.B: Private NAT gateways are for connecting to other VPCs or on-premises networks, not the public internet.
others.D: Private NAT gateways cannot provide internet access regardless of subnet.

tip: Public NAT gateway lives in a public subnet; private subnets route to it.

why: An SCP attached directly to each of the three nonproduction member accounts restricts only those accounts. Alternatively, moving the nonproduction accounts into a new OU and attaching the SCP to that OU applies the restriction to them while leaving the production account unaffected.

others.A: Attaching to the root OU would also restrict the production account.
others.C: SCPs do not affect the management account, so this restricts nothing.
others.D: Attaching the SCP to a production OU restricts the wrong account.

tip: SCPs never restrict the management account; scope them with OUs or direct account attachment.

why: A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 keeps traffic between the EC2 instances and S3 on the AWS network without traversing the internet. A bucket policy with an aws:SourceVpce condition allows access only from that endpoint, securing the classified data.

others.B: An IAM policy grants permission but does not make the network path private.
others.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic to S3's public endpoints over the internet path.
others.D: Static access keys are a credential (and a poor practice on EC2), not a private connection.

tip: Private EC2-to-S3 = VPC endpoint + bucket policy restricting aws:SourceVpce.

why: Adding Aurora reader instances scales out read capacity and provides additional failover targets, with no downtime to add them. RDS Proxy pools connections and reduces failover time by keeping client connections open, improving scalability and availability for the heavy load.

others.A: Logging state changes with EventBridge and Lambda provides monitoring, not additional capacity.
others.B: Zero-downtime restart relates to patching, and Database Activity Streams monitor activity; neither adds capacity.
others.D: Replicating Aurora to Redis with DMS is complex, not a standard caching pattern, and does not help write load.

tip: Aurora read scaling = more readers; connection storms and faster failover = RDS Proxy.

why: A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint forwards DNS queries from the VPC to on-premises DNS servers over the VPN. A forwarding resolver rule for the on-premises domain, associated with the VPC, lets resources resolve private on-premises records without exposing them publicly.

others.B: An inbound endpoint lets on-premises systems resolve AWS-hosted names, the opposite direction.
others.C: A private hosted zone would require duplicating on-premises records in AWS rather than resolving them from the on-premises DNS.
others.D: A public hosted zone exposes internal service records on the internet, which is insecure.

tip: VPC -> on-prem DNS = outbound endpoint; on-prem -> VPC DNS = inbound endpoint.

why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each photo between access tiers based on its own access pattern, handling photos popular for months and those viewed for a week, with no retrieval fees. DynamoDB stores the metadata and S3 location for fast queries to decide which photos to display.

others.A: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so 20 MB photos cannot be stored, and it is costly for blobs.
others.C: A fixed 30-day transition does not fit photos that stay popular for months, and object tags are not queryable metadata storage.
others.D: Glacier classes require restores and are unsuitable for photos users view on demand.

tip: Unknown or varying access patterns = S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

why: The least outstanding requests (LOR) algorithm on an ALB target group routes each new request to the target with the fewest in-flight requests, so overloaded instances receive fewer new requests. RequestCountPerTarget and ActiveConnectionCount are the CloudWatch metrics that show per-target load to confirm the effect.

others.A: Round robin ignores how busy each target is, so overloaded instances keep receiving requests.
others.C: Round robin does not account for outstanding requests on each target.
others.D: LOR is right, but RequestCount and TargetResponseTime are aggregate metrics that do not show per-target load as directly.

tip: Uneven request durations on ALB = least outstanding requests routing.

why: AWS Budgets supports Savings Plans coverage budgets: you set a coverage target threshold and a daily period, and Budgets sends notifications when coverage falls below it. It is fully managed, so no code is required.

others.B: A custom Lambda report with SES requires building and maintaining code.
others.C: A Budgets report delivers periodic reports but does not alert when coverage drops below a threshold.
others.D: Savings Plans alert subscriptions notify about expirations and renewals of plans, not coverage drops.

tip: Coverage or utilization alerts for RIs/Savings Plans = AWS Budgets coverage/utilization budgets.

why: Amazon MSK supports public access only for clusters in public subnets with public access turned on, and it requires TLS encryption in transit with an authentication method such as mutual TLS (or SASL/SCRAM, IAM). Adding public subnets to the existing VPC and enabling mutual TLS is the most direct path.

others.B: Creating a new VPC adds work and network reconfiguration without benefit.
others.C: MSK uses the Kafka protocol, not HTTP, and an internal ALB restricted to the VPC CIDR is not public.
others.D: An NLB in private subnets is internal, and Kafka clients need broker-level addressing that a simple HTTPS listener does not provide.

tip: MSK public access requires public subnets, TLS in transit and an auth method enabled.

why: An internal Transfer Family SFTP endpoint in two AZs is reachable from on premises over the existing private connectivity, keeping it secure and resilient. Storing files in S3 and using a Transfer Family managed workflow to invoke Lambda processes each order file immediately on upload.

others.A: An internet-facing endpoint is unnecessary exposure when private connectivity exists, making it less secure.
others.B: A single AZ is not resilient, and the endpoint is unnecessarily internet facing.
others.C: Periodic scheduled polling does not process orders immediately.

tip: Transfer Family managed workflows trigger post-upload processing; internal endpoints for private access.

why: AWS Outposts brings AWS infrastructure on premises, and Amazon EMR can run on Outposts. This keeps data processing in the data center while gaining managed, scalable Hadoop and Spark clusters with less operational complexity.

others.A: Running EMR in the Region moves the processing to AWS, violating the on-premises requirement.
others.B: DataSync copies data to AWS, so processing would happen in the cloud, not on premises.
others.D: Snowball migrates data to S3, again moving the processing to AWS.

tip: Must stay on premises but want AWS services = Outposts.

why: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves the same data over both SMB and NFS to Windows, macOS and Linux clients. Its auto tiering policy moves cold data automatically from SSD to the lower-cost capacity pool tier, fitting the mix of frequent and infrequent access with minimal management.

others.A: Amazon EFS supports NFS only, not SMB for Windows clients.
others.C: S3 File Gateway is designed for on-premises access, adding a gateway to manage for in-Region EC2 clients.
others.D: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS but not SMB multi-protocol access.

tip: SMB + NFS together = FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

why: Decomposing the monolith into microservices on Amazon ECS lets each module be updated, deployed and scaled independently with rolling deployments, minimizing downtime. Service auto scaling adjusts capacity, and long-running 20-minute report jobs are not limited the way Lambda would be.

others.A: Lambda's 15-minute maximum timeout cannot run 20-minute reports, and a single function keeps the monolith.
others.B: Spot interruptions would force report generation to restart, increasing disruption.
others.D: A single environment with all-at-once deployments causes downtime on every update.

tip: Lambda max timeout is 15 minutes; microservices on containers for gradual modernization.

why: AWS Lambda natively supports Python, scales automatically to handle hundreds of requests per second, and requires no servers to provision or manage. This makes it the serverless microservice option with minimal infrastructure and operational support.

others.A: A Spot Fleet of EC2 instances requires managing servers and handling Spot interruptions, and is not serverless.
others.B: Elastic Beanstalk still runs and manages EC2 instances under the hood, so it is not serverless.
others.C: EKS with self-managed EC2 nodes involves significant cluster and node management.

tip: Serverless microservice with minimal ops = Lambda (often behind API Gateway).

why: A transit gateway associated with a Direct Connect gateway over a transit VIF gives on premises a single connection to all 30 VPCs. With VPC attachments and route propagation, every VPC can reach every other VPC and on premises through one centrally managed hub.

others.B: A Direct Connect gateway with virtual private gateways connects VPCs to on premises but does not enable VPC-to-VPC traffic.
others.C: A full mesh of peering connections among 30 VPCs is a lot of connections and route table management.
others.D: Thirty separate VPN connections add overhead, do not connect VPCs to each other, and ignore Direct Connect.

tip: DX + many VPCs needing full connectivity = transit VIF -> DX gateway -> Transit Gateway.

why: Default Host Management Configuration lets Systems Manager manage all EC2 instances in the Region automatically using an account-level role, without changing the instances' existing IAM instance profiles. The instances can then be patched while the RDS access role stays intact, so applications are not disrupted.

others.A: An EC2 instance can have only one instance profile (one role), so you cannot attach a second role alongside the existing one.
others.B: Systems Manager does not use IAM users to manage EC2 instances; the SSM Agent needs role credentials.
others.D: Removing the existing policies would break the applications' access to RDS.

tip: SSM without touching instance roles = Default Host Management Configuration (needs IMDSv2 and recent agent); otherwise add AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore to the existing role.

why: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales pods but not nodes. The Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler watches for pods that cannot be scheduled due to insufficient capacity and adjusts the node group's Auto Scaling group size automatically, with little administration.

others.A: Scaling on node memory usage is a manual or custom metric approach that does not react to unschedulable pods.
others.C: A custom Lambda function to resize the cluster adds code and maintenance.
others.D: An Auto Scaling group alone is not aware of pending Kubernetes pods; it needs Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) to drive it.

tip: HPA scales pods; Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter scales nodes.

why: When multipart uploads are interrupted or never completed, the uploaded parts remain stored and billed but are invisible as objects. A Lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload deletes those orphaned parts after a set number of days, stopping the growing storage cost.

others.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances but costs extra and does not remove orphaned parts.
others.C: S3 Inventory reports on objects; it does not prevent archiving or remove storage.
others.D: CloudFront caches content for delivery; it does not reduce the objects stored in S3.

tip: Rising S3 cost with constant object counts = incomplete multipart uploads; add an abort lifecycle rule.

why: ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond reads and writes in memory and includes native geospatial commands (GEOADD, GEOSEARCH) suited to live latitude and longitude tracking. Placing it in front of PostgreSQL offloads the high-frequency location reads and writes as the user base grows.

others.A: Multi-AZ adds high availability, not read or write performance, and the standby cannot serve traffic.
others.B: OpenSearch Service is built for search and analytics, not rapid transactional updates as the primary store.
others.C: DAX works only with DynamoDB and cannot cache an RDS for PostgreSQL database.

tip: DAX is DynamoDB-only; Redis has built-in geospatial support.

why: DynamoDB deletion protection prevents a table from being deleted by anyone until the setting is explicitly turned off. It is a simple table setting that directly prevents the disruption, with the least operational overhead.

others.A: A CloudTrail, EventBridge and Lambda restore pipeline is complex, and a deleted table cannot be restored without backups.
others.B: Backups help recovery but still cause disruption and require manual restore work.
others.D: Point-in-time recovery aids recovery after the fact but does not prevent the deletion or the resulting disruption.

tip: Prevent accidental deletion = deletion protection; recover = PITR or backups.

why: Storage Gateway cached volumes keep the primary data in Amazon S3, freeing on-premises capacity, while caching frequently accessed data locally for low-latency retrieval. Local cache hits need no transfer, minimizing bandwidth costs, and there are no retrieval fees for data in S3.

others.A: Glacier expedited retrieval and provisioned capacity cost extra, violating the no-additional-cost retrieval requirement.
others.C: Stored volumes keep the full dataset on premises, so they do not relieve the storage capacity shortage.
others.D: Direct Connect adds cost, and stored volumes still keep all data on premises.

tip: Cached volumes = primary in AWS, hot data local; stored volumes = primary local, async backup to AWS.

why: Predictive scaling analyzes historical daily and weekly load to forecast capacity and launch instances ahead of demand. Combining it with dynamic target tracking scaling handles real-time deviations from the forecast, meeting both requirements.

others.A: Step scaling only reacts to live CPU changes and does not use historical forecasting.
others.C: Scheduled scaling uses fixed times you define, not automated analysis of trends or reaction to live changes.
others.D: Simple scaling with cooldowns is reactive, slow, and uses no forecast.

tip: Forecast + live adjustments = predictive scaling plus target tracking.

why: The load comes from repeated identical reads, which ElastiCache for Redis can serve from memory with sub-millisecond latency instead of hitting Aurora. Caching these results removes most of the read load at lower cost than continually adding replicas.

others.B: Another read replica only adds capacity temporarily, as already observed, and costs more as load grows.
others.C: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas as load grows, increasing cost without addressing the repetitive reads.
others.D: Multiple writers do not address a read-heavy workload, and Aurora MySQL multi-master is no longer supported for new clusters.

tip: Repeated identical reads = cache (ElastiCache); not more replicas.

why: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default and may not reflect a recent write. Setting ConsistentRead to true requests strongly consistent reads that always return the most recent data, at double the read capacity cost, which is acceptable since latency is fine.

others.A: DynamoDB has no read replicas within a Region; global table replicas are eventually consistent.
others.B: Global secondary indexes support only eventually consistent reads.
others.D: Eventually consistent reads are the default and cause the stale data problem.

tip: Stale DynamoDB reads = use strongly consistent reads (not supported on GSIs or across global table Regions).

why: AWS WAF provides managed rule groups that block SQL injection, cross-site scripting and other web attacks before they reach the application. RDS parameter groups allow database security settings, such as enforcing SSL connections, to be configured centrally without managing servers.

others.A: Security groups and NACLs filter by IP, port and protocol and cannot inspect requests for SQL injection.
others.C: Network Firewall can do some inspection but is more complex to deploy and manage than WAF for web attacks.
others.D: Separate database accounts limit privileges but do not block SQL injection or web exploits.

tip: SQL injection / XSS protection = AWS WAF (layer 7).

why: GuardDuty RDS Protection analyzes Aurora login activity and detects anomalous behaviour such as unusual failed or incomplete login attempts. It can be enabled across member accounts from a delegated administrator in Organizations, with no agents or log pipelines to manage.

others.A: SCPs restrict permissions; they do not detect or report login attempts.
others.C: Exporting general logs to S3 requires building custom analysis to detect anomalies.
others.D: CloudTrail records AWS API calls, not database login attempts.

tip: Anomalous Aurora logins = GuardDuty RDS Protection.

why: A Direct Connect gateway is a global resource that connects virtual private gateways in multiple Regions to Direct Connect connections. Attaching both companies' DX connections and VPC virtual private gateways to the DX gateway gives scalable connectivity between the data centers and the VPCs in both Regions.

others.A: VPC peering does not provide connectivity to the data centers and scales poorly.
others.B: A private VIF connects to a single virtual private gateway in one Region unless a Direct Connect gateway is used.
others.C: Self-managed VPN appliances on EC2 add significant operational overhead.

tip: Direct Connect to VPCs in multiple Regions = Direct Connect gateway.

why: Kinesis Data Streams absorbs large traffic spikes and preserves ordering of records within each shard. Lambda processes the stream serverlessly, and DynamoDB stores the processed updates in a highly available, fully managed database, minimizing management.

others.B: EC2 consumers require server management, and Redshift is a data warehouse, not a low-latency leaderboard store.
others.C: SNS does not guarantee ordering for standard topics, and a SQL database on EC2 requires management.
others.D: A standard SQS queue does not guarantee ordering, and EC2 workers add management overhead.

tip: Ordered streaming ingestion with spikes = Kinesis Data Streams (per-shard order).

why: S3 Same-Region Replication automatically copies new log objects from each account's bucket to a central bucket in us-west-2, keeping data in the Region. It is fully managed, supports cross-account replication, and requires no custom code.

others.A: S3 Lifecycle policies transition or expire objects; they cannot copy objects to another bucket.
others.C: A daily script copying entire buckets is wasteful, costly in requests, and adds operational overhead.
others.D: Lambda functions in every account add code to maintain and per-invocation cost.

tip: Copy objects automatically within a Region = SRR; across Regions = CRR.

why: An S3 Multi-Region Access Point gives one global endpoint that routes both uploads and downloads to the closest bucket over the AWS network, so using its ARN for streaming and uploads minimizes latency in each Region. Because uploads can land in any of the three buckets, two-way (bidirectional) replication keeps all buckets in sync.

others.A: One-way replication from us-east-2 cannot propagate uploads that land in eu-west-2 or ap-southeast-1 buckets.
others.B: Chained one-way replication does not sync uploads made to the ap-southeast-1 or eu-west-2 buckets back to the others.
others.D: Leaving uploads on the us-east-2 bucket keeps upload latency high for developers near the other Regions.

tip: Multi-Region Access Point for active-active reads and writes needs bidirectional replication.

why: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location and then over the optimized AWS backbone to the bucket, reducing upload latency for users far from the bucket. Content is stored in S3 in the Region where it is consumed, which suits the local nature of the news.

others.A: CloudFront is optimized for content delivery; using it for uploads (PUT/POST) is possible but not the purpose-built way to accelerate S3 uploads.
others.C: Uploading to EC2 and then copying to S3 adds servers, latency and operational burden.
others.D: Multiple CloudFront distributions add complexity and improve downloads rather than upload latency.

tip: Faster long-distance uploads to S3 = Transfer Acceleration.

why: An SNS topic fans out each message to multiple subscriber SQS queues, and SNS subscription filter policies ensure each queue, and therefore each target Lambda function, receives only the messages it needs. SQS adds buffering and retries, and Lambda polls the queues through managed event source mappings.

others.B: EventBridge with rules can also filter and route to Lambda, but this bank's key prefers the SNS fan-out with filtering pattern; in practice EventBridge is also a reasonable choice.
others.C: MSK requires cluster management and does not provide simple per-consumer message filtering.
others.D: Sending to multiple SQS queues directly from API Gateway requires separate integrations and has no built-in filtering.

tip: Fan-out with per-subscriber filtering = SNS filter policies (often SNS -> SQS -> Lambda).

why: An S3 Inventory report can list objects with their encryption status so unencrypted objects can be identified. S3 Batch Operations can then copy each object in place with new encryption settings, and default encryption is configured so future objects are also encrypted.

others.B: Storage Lens gives aggregate metrics, not per-object lists, and SSE-KMS does not use a customer-provided key.
others.C: The usage report does not list objects, AWS Batch is not the S3 Batch Operations service, and SSE-KMS is not a customer-provided key.
others.D: The usage report cannot identify unencrypted objects and this does nothing to encrypt existing objects.

tip: Find unencrypted objects = S3 Inventory; re-encrypt at scale = S3 Batch Operations copy.
flag: S3 default bucket encryption only supports SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS, not SSE-C, and S3 now disables SSE-C on new buckets by default, so A cannot work exactly as written; it is still the closest option, but in practice a customer managed KMS key (or imported key material) with SSE-KMS would be used.

why: Route 53 public hosted zones provide highly available, managed authoritative DNS for internet domains on AWS. Importing the existing zone file into a new public hosted zone and then updating the registrar's name servers migrates the DNS records rapidly.

others.B: A private hosted zone answers only queries from associated VPCs, so the public website would not resolve on the internet.
others.C: Simple AD and Directory Service provide directory DNS for internal domains, not public authoritative DNS hosting.
others.D: A Resolver inbound endpoint answers queries from on-premises networks into a VPC; it still depends on the failing provider.

tip: Public website DNS on AWS = Route 53 public hosted zone; import a zone file to migrate quickly.

why: AWS AppConfig is a managed service for storing, validating and deploying application configuration. AWS Secrets Manager securely stores credentials for RDS and other services, supports retrieval via API and offers built-in rotation, giving the least administrative overhead.

others.B: Lambda is a compute service, not a configuration store; Parameter Store can hold secrets but lacks built-in rotation.
others.C: Self-managed encrypted files in S3 require custom handling for access, encryption and rotation.
others.D: Amazon RDS is not a service for storing and retrieving application or service credentials.

tip: App config = AppConfig; credentials with rotation = Secrets Manager.

why: RDS for MySQL supports TLS connections using certificates signed by the RDS certificate authority. Downloading the AWS-provided root (CA bundle) certificates and using them in all client connections, optionally enforcing require_secure_transport, encrypts data in transit.

others.A: IAM database authentication controls how users authenticate; it does not by itself enforce encryption of all application traffic.
others.B: RDS does not let you install self-signed server certificates; clients must trust the RDS CA certificates.
others.C: Restoring a snapshot with encryption enabled addresses encryption at rest, which is already enabled.

tip: RDS in-transit encryption = use RDS CA certificates for TLS; at-rest encryption must be set at creation.

why: A Network Load Balancer can be assigned one Elastic IP address per Availability Zone subnet, giving clients fixed IP addresses to allow on their firewalls. The NLB then distributes traffic to the EC2 instances.

others.B: Application Load Balancers do not support Elastic IP addresses; their IPs change.
others.C: An A record pointing to an Elastic IP would bypass the load balancer, since you cannot attach that EIP to an ALB.
others.D: A single proxy instance is a single point of failure and adds management overhead.

tip: Static IPs for a load balancer = NLB with Elastic IPs (or Global Accelerator in front of an ALB).

why: Best practice is to protect the root user with MFA and avoid using it for daily tasks. Creating IAM users or roles for administrative work limits root use to the few tasks that require it.

others.A: The root user of a standalone account cannot simply be disabled; it is needed for certain account-level tasks.
others.C: Root access keys should never be created; they grant unrestricted access and are a major security risk.
others.D: Sharing root credentials for daily administration violates least privilege and best practice.

tip: Root user: enable MFA, no access keys, use only for root-only tasks.

why: Enhanced networking (ENA) provides higher bandwidth, higher packets per second and lower latency between instances. A cluster placement group places instances close together in one AZ on a low-latency, high-throughput network segment, minimizing node-to-node latency.

others.B: Separating instances into different accounts adds no network performance benefit.
others.D: Multiple ENIs provide more interfaces or subnets, not lower latency between nodes.
others.E: EBS-optimized instances improve storage I/O throughput, not inter-node network latency.

tip: Lowest inter-node latency = cluster placement group + enhanced networking (ENA/EFA).

why: FSx for Windows File Server provides native SMB file shares with the same directory semantics, so applications keep working without changes. AWS DataSync efficiently migrates millions of small files and deep directory trees from SMB sources, preserving metadata, with little operational effort.

others.A: Direct Connect is a network link, not a migration tool, and S3 is object storage, which would require application changes.
others.B: FSx for Lustre does not provide SMB access, so applications would need to change.
others.D: A volume gateway exposes iSCSI block volumes, not SMB file shares.

tip: SMB workloads with no app changes = FSx for Windows File Server; migrate with DataSync.

why: CloudWatch cross-account observability lets a monitoring account act as a sink that can view and query metrics, logs and traces from linked source accounts. The monitoring account provides a CloudFormation template (or Organizations-wide setup) that each source account deploys to link and share its data.

others.B: SCPs only limit permissions; they cannot grant access or share CloudWatch data.
others.C: Policies in other accounts cannot be attached to an IAM user in the monitoring account, and this does not enable a unified CloudWatch view.
others.D: IAM policies are account-scoped and cannot be attached to users in another account; this is not how CloudWatch cross-account works.

tip: Central monitoring account across an organization = CloudWatch cross-account observability (OAM sinks and links).

why: AWS WAF is already protecting the CloudFront distribution, so adding an IP set match rule that blocks the malicious IP stops it at the edge. Because CloudFront is in front, the ALB and instances see CloudFront IPs, so blocking must happen in WAF.

others.A: CloudFront distributions do not have network ACLs.
others.C: Behind CloudFront and the ALB, the instances receive traffic from the ALB, not the client IP, so a NACL rule would not match.
others.D: Security groups only support allow rules and cannot deny specific IPs.

tip: Block a client IP behind CloudFront = WAF IP set rule; security groups cannot deny.

why: IAM Identity Center integrates with an external IdP via SAML 2.0 and SCIM to provision users and groups automatically. Permission sets then grant thousands of employees access across all 10 accounts in the organization, using the existing IdP for authentication.

others.A: Creating thousands of IAM users per account is unmanageable and defeats federation.
others.B: Root users must never be shared or used for employee access.
others.D: AWS RAM shares resources such as subnets or transit gateways, not account access for users.

tip: Workforce SSO across Organizations accounts with an existing IdP = IAM Identity Center.

why: AdministratorAccess is an AWS managed identity-based policy that grants full access to all AWS services and resources. Attaching it to an IAM user group and adding the five users gives them full access with central management.

others.A: AdministratorAccess is an identity-based policy; resource-based policies are attached to resources, not to IAM groups.
others.B: SystemAdministrator is a job-function policy with limited permissions, not full access.
others.D: SystemAdministrator is not full access, and resource-based policies cannot be attached to groups.

tip: IAM groups take identity-based policies only; full access = AdministratorAccess.

why: SQS FIFO queues provide exactly-once processing and ordered delivery with deduplication, replacing the middleware's guarantee. AWS Lambda runs the compute tiers without any servers to manage, minimizing infrastructure management.

others.B: EC2 instances require managing servers, patching and scaling.
others.C: Standard SNS topics provide at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once.
others.E: EKS still requires cluster and container management compared with Lambda.

tip: Exactly-once messaging on AWS = SQS FIFO (or SNS FIFO to SQS FIFO).

why: AWS Transfer Family for SFTP is a fully managed, multi-AZ SFTP endpoint, and Amazon EFS provides highly available, regional file storage that keeps the existing file-system workflow. An Auto Scaling group with scheduled scaling launches the batch EC2 instance only for the nightly run, minimizing operational effort.

others.B: A self-managed SFTP server on one EC2 instance with a single-AZ EBS volume is neither highly available nor low effort.
