others.C: Running and patching your own SFTP service on EC2 adds operational effort compared with Transfer Family.
others.D: S3 works with Transfer Family, but the application would need to be modified to pull files from S3, adding effort.

tip: Managed SFTP = Transfer Family (backed by S3 or EFS).

why: AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and routes users to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint, improving availability and performance. Application Load Balancers in each Region handle HTTP traffic and support AWS WAF to block common web exploits.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be attached to Network Load Balancers.
others.C: WAF cannot be deployed on NLBs, and CloudFront does not provide static IP addresses.
others.D: CloudFront does not offer static IP addresses for clients to allow, and a Route 53 latency record cannot be a CloudFront origin in this way.

tip: Static IPs + WAF for HTTP apps across Regions = Global Accelerator in front of ALBs with WAF.

why: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections, eliminating 'too many connections' errors. It also maintains client connections during failover and routes to the new writer without waiting for DNS propagation, reducing Aurora failover times by up to 66%, well beyond the 20% goal.

others.A: Moving to RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters is a migration away from Aurora and does not solve connection exhaustion.
others.C: DynamoDB with DAX would require a complete application and data model rewrite.
others.D: Redshift is a data warehouse, not a transactional replacement, and relocation is unrelated to failover of Aurora.

tip: RDS Proxy: connection pooling + faster failover.

why: S3 Object Lambda Access Points run a Lambda function on each GET request to transform the data on the fly, here redacting PII before returning it. The provider reads any file, including the newest, through the access point, and it scales automatically with no copies to manage.

others.B: A custom web application on EC2 must be built, scaled and maintained, adding significant overhead.
others.D: Building a DynamoDB pipeline to extract non-PII data adds development and storage overhead and changes how the provider accesses conversations.

tip: Redact or transform S3 data on read without copies = S3 Object Lambda.

why: A CloudWatch alarm with the EC2 recover action automatically recovers the instance onto new hardware when system status checks fail, keeping its instance ID, private IP, Elastic IP and EBS volumes. This improves recovery time for a single-instance system without code changes.

others.A: Termination protection only prevents accidental termination; it does not help recovery from failures.
others.B: EC2 instances have no Multi-AZ deployment option, and the system cannot run on more than one instance.
others.D: RAID across EBS volumes protects storage only, not recovery from host or instance failure.

tip: Single EC2 instance, faster recovery = CloudWatch alarm EC2 recover action (or simplified automatic recovery).

why: Amazon ECS runs the existing containers with minimal changes. ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking keeps at least three tasks, and the spread placement strategy on the attribute:ecs.availability-zone distributes tasks across the three AZs for high availability.

others.B: Self-managed EKS nodes require managing node lifecycle and patching, adding operational overhead.
others.C: Plain EC2 instances do not run container workloads in a managed way, and Reserved Instances are a pricing choice, not an HA design.
others.D: Lambda requires refactoring the containerized application into functions, and minimum capacity of 3 is not a Lambda concept.

tip: ECS task spread across AZs: placement strategy spread on attribute:ecs.availability-zone.

why: Keeping newer, high-demand movies in S3 Standard and older, less-requested movies in S3 Standard-IA lowers storage cost for the older titles. Standard-IA still provides millisecond access, so older movies can be streamed immediately, well within 5 minutes of purchase.

others.A: Moving data per movie based on fluctuating demand is not something Lifecycle rules can track; they work on object age, not demand.
others.C: Glacier Flexible Retrieval expedited retrieval usually takes 1-5 minutes but is not guaranteed without provisioned capacity, and files up to 10 GB add retrieval cost.
others.D: Bulk retrieval from Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes 5-12 hours, missing the 5-minute requirement.

tip: Need fast access to rarely used objects = Standard-IA; Glacier retrieval times rarely fit minutes-level SLAs.

why: ECS on Fargate is serverless and runs any Docker image. Mounting an Amazon EFS volume in the task definition provides 50 GB or more of shared, elastic storage for temporary files with no servers to manage (Fargate ephemeral storage up to 200 GiB is also an option).

others.A: Lambda cannot mount S3 as a volume, and its /tmp storage is limited to 10 GB.
others.B: Lambda cannot attach EBS volumes.
others.D: The EC2 launch type requires managing container instances, so it is not serverless.

tip: Lambda ephemeral storage max is 10 GB; Fargate supports up to 200 GiB plus EFS.

why: Because the LDAP directory does not support SAML, a custom identity broker authenticates users against LDAP and then calls AWS STS (AssumeRole or GetFederationToken) to obtain temporary credentials. The broker can generate a console sign-in URL from those credentials for console access.

others.A: IAM Identity Center federates with SAML 2.0 IdPs or AD via AWS Directory Service; it cannot connect directly to a non-SAML LDAP directory.
others.B: IAM policies cannot be integrated into LDAP for authentication.
others.C: Rotating long-term IAM credentials whenever LDAP changes is insecure and complex, and still is not federation.

tip: Non-SAML identity store = custom identity broker with STS temporary credentials.

why: Recycle Bin supports EBS-backed AMIs: a retention rule keeps deregistered AMIs for a set period, so accidentally deleted AMIs can be restored quickly. It requires only a one-time rule configuration, giving the least operational overhead.

others.A: Snapshots of AMIs in another account require rebuilding and re-registering AMIs, which is slower and more effort.
others.B: Periodically copying AMIs to another account adds ongoing work and cost.
others.D: AMIs are not uploaded to S3 buckets for replication; this is not a supported recovery method.

tip: Recover accidentally deleted EBS snapshots or AMIs = Recycle Bin retention rules.

why: At 100 Mbps only at night, uploading 150 TB would take many months. Multiple Snowball Edge devices (about 80 TB usable each) can be shipped, loaded and returned within the month, and are far cheaper than Snowmobile for this volume.

others.A: Snowmobile was intended for 10 PB-scale migrations, is overkill for 150 TB, and has been discontinued.
others.C: Transfer Acceleration does not increase the limited 100 Mbps nightly bandwidth.
others.D: A VPN and VPC endpoint still rely on the same slow link and cannot move 150 TB in a month.

tip: Quick math: 100 Mbps is about 1 TB per day at full utilization; tens to hundreds of TB on limited links = Snowball.

why: Keeping a public web tier and private application tier on EC2 mirrors the existing architecture with minimal changes. Aurora MySQL is MySQL-compatible, supports point-in-time recovery from continuous backups, and is fully managed in private subnets, minimizing operational overhead.

others.A: Putting the web tier in private subnets would require adding a load balancer or other changes for internet access.
others.C: RDS for MySQL also supports point-in-time recovery, but the key prefers Aurora MySQL for its managed storage and resilience with lower overhead.
others.D: Placing the database and all tiers in public subnets is insecure.

tip: Both RDS and Aurora support PITR; never put databases in public subnets.

why: An SQS access policy is a resource-based policy on the queue that can grant another AWS account's principals permissions such as sqs:ReceiveMessage. The other company keeps using its own identities and permissions without assuming a role in the development team's account.

others.A: Instance profiles attach roles to EC2 instances in the same account and do not grant cross-account queue access.
others.B: An IAM identity policy in the development team's account cannot grant permissions to principals in another account.
others.D: An SNS access policy controls an SNS topic, not access to an SQS queue.

tip: Cross-account access without assuming a role = resource-based policy (SQS queue policy).

why: With the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy on the instance role, the SSM Agent (preinstalled on Amazon Linux) connects outbound through the NAT gateway. Developers then use Session Manager, including SSH tunneling through it, from anywhere with IAM authentication and logging, without bastion hosts or open inbound ports, and with no extra charge.

others.A: A bastion host in a private subnet is unreachable from the internet, and ec2:CreateVpnConnection is unrelated to SSH access.
others.B: Site-to-Site VPN costs money per hour and still requires a separate solution for remote developers.
others.C: A bastion host costs money to run, requires key management, and exposes SSH to the internet.

tip: Secure shell access without bastions or open ports = Session Manager.

why: Storage Gateway volume gateway with cached volumes stores the full dataset in Amazon S3 while keeping frequently accessed subsets cached locally for low-latency access. This removes the need to buy more on-premises storage arrays, reducing capital expenses.

others.A: Migrating data to S3 with DataSync leaves researchers without low-latency local access to the working subset.
others.B: File gateway also caches data locally, but the data currently resides on block storage arrays, which map more directly to volume gateway cached volumes.
others.D: EFS over a VPN gives higher-latency access for researchers and no local cache.

tip: Block storage arrays to cloud with local cache = cached volume gateway.

why: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery continuously backs up the table and lets you restore to any second within the last 35 days, covering the 24-hour requirement. It is enabled with a single setting, giving the least operational overhead.

others.B: AWS Backup schedules backups at intervals, so it cannot restore to an arbitrary point unless you also enable continuous backups, adding configuration.
others.C: Hourly on-demand backups via Lambda only allow restoring to hourly points and require custom code.
others.D: Streams hold changes for only 24 hours and require building a custom replay mechanism to restore.

tip: Restore DynamoDB to any second in the last 35 days = PITR.
